title: What Alabama Athletics was Like When Grand Theft Auto V was Released: Just a Minute - Yahoo Sports

title: Section 6213(a) Deficiency Petitions After Laurenzano v. Commissioner: The Fourth Circuit Reaffirms Equitable Tolling and Dismantles the First Circuit’s Mandatory Rule - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. Laurenzano v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, No. 25-2020. 4th Circuit, November 18, 2026 For decades, tax controversy practitioners operated under an unyielding procedural orthodoxy: the 90-day deadline under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 6213(a) to petition the United States Tax Court for a redetermination of a deficiency was strictly jurisdictional. Under that regime, missing the deadline by a single day slammed the courthouse doors shut, precluding any judicial review prior to assessment and payment. That foundational assumption has rapidly eroded. On November 18, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit issued its published opinion in Laurenzano v. Commissioner, firmly holding that the statutory filing deadline in I.R.C. § 6213(a) is an ordinary, nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule and that it is subject to the traditional presumption of equitable tolling. In reaching this conclusion, the Fourth Circuit aligned itself with the Second, Third, Sixth, and Eighth Circuits, while directly confronting and rejecting the First Circuit’s contrary decision in Kyick Holdings, LLC v. Commissioner, which had classified the deadline as nonjurisdictional yet strictly mandatory. For CPAs and Enrolled Agents representing clients before the Internal Revenue Service and evaluating Tax Court litigation strategies, Laurenzano provides an authoritative synthesis of modern jurisdictional jurisprudence and offers critical procedural tools for salvaging deficiency petitions caught in extraordinary circumstances. The controversy in Laurenzano v. Commissioner arose from a routine statutory notice of deficiency issued under I.R.C. § 6212(a). On September 9, 2024, the IRS mailed a notice of deficiency to Peter Laurenzano’s residence in Maryland, determining an income tax deficiency of $14,151.87. In conformity with standard IRS deficiency notices, the letter advised Laurenzano that he had 90 days—or 150 days if addressed to a person outside the United States—to contest the proposed deficiency by filing a petition with the Tax Court. According to Laurenzano, when the statutory notice arrived at his Maryland home, he was away on an extended fishing trip spanning Florida and the Bahamas. Operating under the mistaken assumption that his travel to the Bahamas qualified him for the extended foreign-taxpayer deadline, Laurenzano calculated his filing window under the 150-day rule. However, Laurenzano missed even that expanded window: the Tax Court did not receive his petition until February 19, 2025—163 days after the IRS mailed the notice of deficiency. The Commissioner moved to dismiss Laurenzano’s petition for lack of jurisdiction on grounds of untimeliness. In response, Laurenzano requested equitable relief, urging the court to excuse the delay. The Tax Court granted the Commissioner’s motion and dismissed the petition. Relying on historical precedent, the Tax Court held that “even if the 150-day period were determined to apply” to Laurenzano, he failed to file within that timeframe, and the court possessed “no authority to extend this 90 day . . . period” for equitable reasons. Facing an immediate assessment under I.R.C. § 6213(c), Laurenzano timely appealed to the Fourth Circuit under I.R.C. § 7482(a)(1), requesting that the dismissal be vacated and arguing that § 6213(a)’s deadline is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule subject to equitable tolling. Reviewing the Tax Court’s legal conclusions and jurisdictional dismissal de novo (McLane v. Commissioner, 24 F.4th 316, 318 (4th Cir. 2022)), the Fourth Circuit divided its inquiry into two successive questions: first, whether the filing deadline in I.R.C. § 6213(a) is jurisdictional; and second, if nonjurisdictional, whether the deadline is subject to equitable tolling. Writing for a unanimous panel joined by Judges King and Wynn, Judge Agee anchored the court’s jurisdictional analysis in the “demanding” clear-statement rule formulated in Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp., 546 U.S. 500, 515 (2006), and recently reaffirmed in Riley v. Bondi, 606 U.S. 259, 275 (2025). Under this doctrine, a statutory threshold is jurisdictional only if the legislature “clearly states” that the limitation cabins a court’s adjudicatory capacity rather than merely regulating the procedural duties of litigants. As the Supreme Court recognized in Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, 596 U.S. 199, 203 (2022), jurisdictional rules cannot be waived or forfeited, must be policed sua sponte, and forbid equitable exceptions. Conversely, claim-processing rules promote the orderly progress of litigation, may be waived or forfeited, and are presumptively open to equitable tolling. Applying these canons to the text of I.R.C. § 6213(a), the Fourth Circuit scrutinized the operative sentence: “Within 90 days, or 150 days if the notice is addressed to a person outside the United States, after the notice of deficiency authorized in section 6212 is mailed (not counting Saturday, Sunday, or any legal holding in the District of Columbia as the last day), the taxpayer may file a petition with the Tax Court for a redetermination of the deficiency.” Borrowing from the Sixth Circuit’s analysis in Oquendo v. Commissioner, 148 F.4th 820, 831 (6th Cir. 2025), Judge Agee observed that “[n]otably absent from this language is a ‘directive[] to courts,’ a ‘reference to jurisdiction,’ and ‘language demarcat[ing] a court’s power.’” On its face, the text addresses what “the taxpayer may” do within the specified timeframe, speaking directly to party obligations rather than judicial adjudicatory power. The panel reinforced this textual reading by contrasting the first sentence of § 6213(a) with the explicit jurisdictional restriction located two sentences later in the very same subsection: “The Tax Court shall have no jurisdiction to enjoin any action or proceeding or order any refund under this subsection unless a timely petition for a redetermination of the deficiency has been filed and then only in respect of the deficiency that is subject of such petition.” This internal contrast demonstrated that “Congress knew how to connect a deadline and a jurisdictional grant when it so chose.” While Congress explicitly stripped the Tax Court of jurisdiction to grant injunctive relief or issue refunds absent a timely petition, it pointedly declined to attach similar jurisdictional language to the general power to redetermine deficiencies under the first sentence. Citing the Third Circuit’s landmark decision in Culp v. Commissioner, 75 F.4th 196, 202 (3d Cir. 2023), the panel emphasized that this textual disparity confirms Congress deliberately withheld jurisdictional consequences from the deficiency petition deadline. The Fourth Circuit found further statutory proof across the broader Internal Revenue Code, where Congress repeatedly tethered deadlines to express jurisdictional grants—such as I.R.C. § 6015(e)(1)(A) for innocent spouse relief (“and the Tax Court shall have jurisdiction... if such petition is filed” timely) and I.R.C. § 6404(h)(1) for interest abatement actions (“The Tax Court shall have jurisdiction... if such action is brought” timely). Finally, the Fourth Circuit compared § 6213(a) to the Collection Due Process (CDP) deadline reviewed in Boechler, 596 U.S. at 204. In Boechler, I.R.C. § 6330(d)(1) included the filing deadline and the phrase “(and the Tax Court shall have jurisdiction with respect to such matter)” in the exact same sentence. Even with that grammatical proximity, the Supreme Court held that § 6330(d)(1) was nonjurisdictional because multiple plausible readings existed. Judge Agee reasoned: “If the filing deadline in Boechler fell short of being jurisdictional, it is hard to see how the more attenuated 90-day deadline in § 6213(a) is jurisdictional. The statute in Boechler contained at least some grammatical connections between the jurisdictional language and the deadline... But there is no such jurisdictional language at all grammatically related to the 90-day deadline in § 6213(a).” The Commissioner urged the Fourth Circuit to maintain the jurisdictional bar based on prior circuit precedent, including Kiker v. Commissioner, 218 F.2d 389 (4th Cir. 1955), and Lundy v. IRS, 45 F.3d 856 (4th Cir. 1995). The panel flatly refused, classifying those decisions as classic “drive-by jurisdictional rulings” that lack any reasoned textual analysis and warrant “no precedential effect” under Arbaugh, 546 U.S. at 511, and Wilkins v. United States, 598 U.S. 152, 160 (2023). The court also rejected the Eleventh Circuit’s unpublished post-Boechler decision in Allen v. Commissioner, No. 22-12537, 2022 WL 17825934 (11th Cir. Dec. 21, 2022), which had maintained that § 6213(a) remained jurisdictional because Boechler did not directly overrule prior circuit law. Judge Agee pointedly observed that Allen “underestimates the strength and significance of Arbaugh and its progeny, including Boechler.” Addressing the Commissioner’s policy argument that treating § 6213(a) as nonjurisdictional disrupts tax administration and clashes with related Code provisions, the Fourth Circuit held that “ministerial consequences of a nonjurisdictional deadline are not ‘unmistakable evidence, on par with express language addressing the court’s jurisdiction,’ necessary to satisfy a clear-statement rule” (Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, 598 U.S. 411, 418 (2023)). Thus, the panel held that § 6213(a)’s deadline is an ordinary claim-processing rule. Once a time limitation is categorized as nonjurisdictional, it enjoys a robust, long-standing presumption that it is subject to equitable tolling (Boechler, 596 U.S. at 209; Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs, 498 U.S. 89, 95–96 (1990)). The doctrine pauses the running of a limitations period when a litigant demonstrates (1) that they have pursued their rights diligently, and (2) that some extraordinary circumstance stood in their way and prevented timely filing (Lozano v. Montoya Alvarez, 572 U.S. 1, 10 (2014)). This presumption governs unless there is “good reason to believe that Congress did not want the equitable tolling doctrine to apply” (Arellano v. McDonough, 598 U.S. 1, 7 (2023); United States v. Brockamp, 519 U.S. 347, 350 (1997)). As the Supreme Court articulated in Enbridge Energy, LP v. Nessel, 146 S. Ct. 1074, 1082 (2026), a statute can rebut the presumption when it speaks in strict, mandatory terms (such as “shall”), sets forth limitations in an unusually emphatic or highly detailed technical manner, contains an extensive scheme of explicit equitable exceptions, or provides an exceptionally long limitations period (such as the 12-year period in United States v. Beggerly, 524 U.S. 38, 49 (1998)). The Fourth Circuit concluded that § 6213(a) displays none of these rebuttal characteristics. Textually, the statute uses the permissive term “may” rather than mandatory phrasing. Structurally, the 90-day window is relatively short and appears within a statutory framework that is “unusually protective of taxpayers and a scheme in which laymen, unassisted by trained lawyers, often initiate the process” (Boechler, 596 U.S. at 209). A major contribution of the Laurenzano decision is its exhaustive examination of the circuit split regarding whether § 6213(a) can be equitably tolled. While the Second Circuit (Buller v. Commissioner, 160 F.4th 266 (2d Cir. 2025)), Third Circuit (Culp, 75 F.4th at 205), Sixth Circuit (Oquendo, 148 F.4th at 833–34), and Eighth Circuit (Maniktala v. Commissioner, 186 F.4th 548, 555 (8th Cir. 2026)) all held that § 6213(a) permits equitable tolling, the First Circuit broke rank in Kyick Holdings, LLC v. Commissioner, 188 F.4th 39 (1st Cir. 2026). In Kyick Holdings, the First Circuit concluded that § 6213(a) is nonjurisdictional but strictly mandatory, asserting that Congress intended to preclude equitable tolling because nine statutory exceptions throughout the Code already account for equitable considerations. The Fourth Circuit rejected Kyick Holdings as an “outlier” and dismantled its nine-exception framework: First, Judge Agee identified that only four exceptions are genuinely relevant to § 6213(a): These four exceptions, the Fourth Circuit observed, are neither numerous nor highly technical. As Judge Ambro noted in Culp, four exceptions pale in comparison to the six detailed technical limits in Brockamp (governing tax refund claims under § 6511) or the fifteen intricate exceptions in Arellano (governing veterans’ benefits). Second, the Fourth Circuit showed why the remaining five “exceptions” cited by the First Circuit are entirely irrelevant: Third, the Fourth Circuit distinguished the Supreme Court’s ruling in Enbridge Energy. In Enbridge, the Supreme Court held that the civil removal deadline in 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1) was not subject to equitable tolling because it used mandatory “shall” language and was interwoven with six express statutory exceptions that directly modified and incorporated § 1446(b)(1)’s timeline. By contrast, § 6213(a) employs permissive language and lacks interwoven, cross-referencing exceptions that would be rendered superfluous by equitable tolling. The Fourth Circuit’s ruling is best understood alongside key insights from the sister circuit opinions: Applying the law to Peter Laurenzano’s appeal, the Fourth Circuit reversed the Tax Court’s fundamental premises: “The Tax Court erred in dismissing Laurenzano’s petition for lack of jurisdiction. As we have explained, § 6213(a) does not divest the Tax Court of the power to hear an untimely petition based on the 90-day deadline, and consequently the Tax Court also has the authority to apply equitable tolling based on the facts of a particular case.” Because the Tax Court erroneously believed it lacked all adjudicatory authority, it never evaluated Laurenzano’s equitable arguments. Accordingly, the Fourth Circuit vacated the dismissal order and remanded the case for further proceedings. Significantly, the panel explicitly declined to rule on the merits of Laurenzano’s equitable tolling claim: “In holding that equitable tolling is available for petitioners who miss § 6213(a)’s deadline, we offer no view on whether Laurenzano is entitled to any equitable relief in this case. That is a question for the Tax Court on remand, Boechler, 596 U.S. at 211, to determine in the first instance.” Tax practitioners should recognize the formidable hurdle facing Laurenzano on remand. Equitable tolling requires extraordinary external impediments coupled with relentless diligence. It is questionable whether embarking on an extended recreational fishing trip to the Bahamas and misinterpreting the statutory foreign-taxpayer deadline constitutes an “extraordinary circumstance” beyond the taxpayer’s control, or merely an instance of neglect and legal error, which traditionally forecloses equitable tolling (Irwin, 498 U.S. at 96). title: Can “GTA V” Help Scientists Model Climate Change in L.A.? - Nautilus | Science Connected
content: You can’t turn your head without seeing an advertisement for Grand Theft Auto VI. The ad blitz is reaching a crescendo because the highly anticipated eighth installment in the Rockstar Games franchise drops tomorrow, 13 years after the release of its predecessor, GTA V. And after such a long wait, the pressure to deliver is sky high. After all, GTA V featured a meticulous and immersive recreation of Los Angeles (called Los Santos) based on field research, satellite maps, census data, and more. And Rockstar’s remarkable level of detail has stood the test of time, with many players returning to the game while they wait for the sequel. Climate scientists are apparently no different. In a new study published in Geoscience Communication, a team of researchers used the fictional city of Los Santos to model rising sea levels. Read more: “Playing Video Games Makes Us Fully Human” “Many games have now advanced graphically to such an extent that they can reproduce real-world locations almost true-to-life,” study author Paul Nörenberg of Germany’s University of Potsdam said in a statement. “The city is a near-exact replica of the real-life Los Angeles, with all its famous landmarks, neighborhoods, and urban and coastal features.” So Nörenberg and his colleague Hugues Lantuit of the Alfred Wegener Institute inundated the digital city with a series of floods designed to mimic encroaching sea levels under various scenarios based on projections from the U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. “In one scenario, greenhouse gas emissions were significantly reduced by robust climate action, and in another, emissions remained high,” Lantuit explained. The high-emission scenario showed the surrounding coastline creeping into Los Santos and water levels rising almost eight feet by the year 2100. By the simulated year 2300, the water level rose another nine feet, knocking out the city’s sewage treatment plants and gasworks, before finally topping out at almost 27 feet by the year 2500. According to their analysis, close to seven percent of Los Santos was lost to the ocean. The scenario where emissions come under tighter control was a little less dire. In those simulations, the water level only rose seven to nine feet by the year 2500 with a land loss hovering around two percent. Under this model, coastal towns and beaches suffered the brunt of the damage, but key infrastructure located farther inland remained untouched (good news for fans of GTA V’s airport quests). The researchers also compared their simulations of a flooded Los Santos to models of scientifically documented flood risks in the real City of Angels. They were a close match. “The virtual environment of GTA V is therefore not only visually reminiscent of Los Angeles. Its landscape is precise and detailed enough to be used for a scientific analysis of climate impacts,” Lantuit said. Why, though, focus on a made-up city like Los Santos in the first place? According to the team, simulating environments people have an emotional attachment to may make the effects of climate change more tangible to them. “If this familiar, personally explored virtual landscape changes, players can engage with the effects of climate change on an emotional level,” Nörenberg said. “This can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.” It’s possible people have a stronger attachment to a fictional (albeit accurate) representation of a city than they do the real thing. It may sound bleak, but GTA V is the second best-selling video game of all time, with over 225 million copies sold—or over 20 times the population of Los Angeles County. And GTA VI may shatter that record. If so, a new generation could develop a connection to the game’s setting, Vice City. Based on over a decade of research, Vice City is an even more detailed recreation of Miami, Florida, another urban area threatened by climate change. Enjoying Nautilus? title: Players say goodbye to Grand Theft Auto V with one last drive - The Guardian
content:
For more than a decade, GTA Online and its virtual California has hosted the criminal capers of millions of players. As many of them prepare to move on to GTA VI, they are marking the end of an era The virtual streets of Grand Theft Auto Online’s Los Santos will be spared from their usual explosions and high-speed car chases tonight, as hundreds of players meet for a final journey across the video game’s world before the release of Grand Theft Auto VI at midnight. Rockstar Games’ multiplayer criminal sandbox normally prompts hostility between its millions of players by giving them ample access to guns, bombs and fighter jets. But fans took it upon themselves to peacefully cruise across the game world together for “one last drive” in virtual California, before the next chapter in the series arrives. Willy, who goes by zarki_34 online, has played GTA Online for thousands of hours over the last decade. He has organised several of his own final drive events. “[GTA Online] has been part of my life for 13 years … I’m now 26,” he says. “I’ve spent half my life with this game.” His route took players from the centre of the game’s Los Angeles-inspired city, across rugged coastlines and through so-Cal countryside in one singular trip. The gamer from southern France livestreams on TikTok and regularly hosts virtual events: from socials where players show off their in-game vehicles to highly choreographed aeroplane stunts. “Some people have been joining for two years,” he said. “Some have become really close friends and I’ve met some amazing people thanks to this game.” Willy’s social media post about his plans for a final drive in GTA Online quickly went viral. Inspired by the idea, groups across North America and Europe suddenly began to plan their own farewells. Rockstar is not ending support for GTA Online anytime soon, but as millions of players prepare to move on to GTA VI, Willy wanted to celebrate “an end of era”. “For me, it’s not just about driving cars,” he says. “It’s about bringing people together who share the same passion and creating good memories.” GTA Online is the multiplayer version of 2013’s Grand Theft Auto V, and was released two weeks after the single-player game. Despite poor performance and lukewarm reviews from critics at the time, years of updates saw the game grow exponentially in popularity and quality while generating billions of dollars in revenue across three generations of video game consoles, starting on the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3. Dylan, 34, from north London, remembers playing the game before the kinks were ironed out. “Back then, you’d get kicked out of the server before you could really enjoy it,” he said. After taking years away from the game, the busy dad has recently returned to Los Santos in anticipation of GTA VI. “I love the world building of GTA, their whole atmosphere of the game.” Dylan has coordinated his own last drive with strangers online, timing it to coincide with the launch of the franchise’s newest entry so that it would “take us exactly to the moment we can press start on GTA VI”.
 

 In GTA Online, players complete missions and activities to grow their criminal empire, working together to plan, prepare and execute high-octane heists. For Jerry, a 20-year-old from Louisiana, this shared experience with up to 30 players at a time is what makes the game special. “People say this community is toxic – it’s not,” he says. He says he began playing the game alone during Covid, and “started meeting these nice people who would help me along the way”. Jerry was encouraged to keep playing by a close friend he met on the game, who has since died. “He’s the main reason I’m doing [the last drive], the memory of him,” he said. While many are preparing to say goodbye to San Andreas after a decade of play tonight, Jerry is holding out a little longer. He has pre-ordered GTA VI, he said, but won’t be leaving Los Santos just yet: “I’m going to stay in GTA Online for at least six months.” The Guardian has something US newsrooms don’t: guaranteed independence. title: Longhorns WR Emmett Mosley V is putting together a career year - Longhorns Wire
content: As the Longhorns have put together an unforgettable 2026 campaign, many different pieces have stepped up. That includes wide receiver Emmett Mosley V., who has put together the best season of his college career. In his second year in the burnt orange, Mosley has been a key piece of the offense and has avoided the injured list for long stretches. In ten games, the talented junior has set a career high in receiving yards with 541. He is also averaging 15.9 yards per catch, which would be a new career best if the season ended today. While his 34 catches are only the second-highest total of his collegiate career, Mosley has been more explosive with the ball in his hands. With only two games left in the 2026 campaign, the Longhorns veteran has also surpassed his receptions and receiving yards total from last year. In his second season in Steve Sarkisian's offense, Mosley has been a reliable option for Arch Manning and has been productive regardless of the opponent. Currently, Mosley ranks second on the team in receptions and receiving yards behind only Ryan Wingo. That is not a bad place to be for a player who struggled at times last year to stay on the field while learning a new offense. Now that he is healthy, Mosley is showing why he is a difference-maker. With two games left in the regular season, Mosley has a prime chance to build on his success. The Longhorns will round out their season against Arkansas and Texas A&M. Those teams have a combined 8-12 record and have struggled in conference play. That should allow Texas and Mosley to enter the postseason in a good place. For Mosley the focus will be on counting to be a piece that quarterback Arch Manning can trust as the Longhorns move closer to a national title. title: Reassessing The Terminal Canaanite Occupation At Jericho: Sultan IV Or Sultan V? - Associates For Biblical Research
content: Author:                    Bryan Windle Category:                    Conquest of Canaan under Joshua & the Inception of the Period of the Judges 1406-1371 BC Despite more than a century of excavation, the stratum representing the terminal Canaanite occupation of Tell es-Sultan/Jericho during the Late Bronze Age remains disputed. Recent publications have renewed the debate over whether Sultan IV or Sultan V represents Jericho’s terminal Canaanite occupation, with Kennedy (2023) [1] defending the final phase of Stratum IV and Nigro (2023, 2024) [2,3] identifying Stratum V as the final Late Bronze Age settlement. To date, few studies have systematically compared the published archaeological evidence for Sultan IV and Sultan V while also evaluating ancient textual evidence relevant to the possible causes of the site’s Late Bronze Age destruction. Resolving this question clarifies the occupational history of Jericho and refines the chronology of the site’s Late Bronze Age settlement sequence. This article evaluates published excavation data from Sultan IV and Sultan V together with ceramic assemblages from contemporary Levantine sites, radiocarbon evidence, inscriptional finds, and architectural remains. The evidence supports identifying Nigro’s Sultan V as the terminal Canaanite occupation at Tell es-Sultan during the Late Bronze Age and suggests a plausible explanation for its destruction….

title: Hauling Brokers into Court: Liability Under Montgomery v. Caribe Transport - OnLabor
content:
Caroline Koclanes is a student at Harvard Law School and a member of the Labor and Employment Lab. “Trust me, I’m upset with the driver, I’m upset with the carrier, but if we don’t go after the broker, this is going to continue happening.”  These are the words of Marcus Coleman, a truck driver himself whose daughter was almost killed in a truck crash.  The Colemans are suing the broker (the middleman who connects sellers with carriers) for “fail[ing] to perform an in-depth safety review” of the carrier.  “[It] is not hard at all,” Mr. Coleman explained. “Within thirty seconds, we found out how many … violations [the carrier] had, how many suspensions, car accidents.”  Last Term, in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC, the Supreme Court made suits like these possible.  Resolving a circuit split, the Court held that federal law does not bar state-law negligence claims against brokers for trucking crashes –– brokers can be held liable.  This ruling offers hope to an industry that has historically disincentivized safety –– hope for workers and for families like the Colemans. The United States trucking industry moves about 38.8 million tons of freight every day.  The industry is made up of four actors: sellers, brokers, carriers, and drivers.  When a seller (say, Walmart) needs goods moved, it contacts a broker, who connects it to a carrier, who in turn hires a driver to haul the goods.  Brokers are the “transportation industry’s matchmakers, connecting sellers of goods to the carriers who move them.”  Roughly 28,000 brokers arrange transportation for more than 780,000 carriers, which employ 3.58 million drivers. Brokers are often well-capitalized –– some Fortune 500 companies with over $16 billion in annual revenue.  In contrast, most carriers are small (91.5% operate fewer than ten trucks) and judgment-proof (the carrier cannot afford to pay damages in a lawsuit).  Federal regulations require carriers to hold only $750,000 in liability insurance, a sum inadequate given the catastrophic nature of many trucking injuries, which can easily reach eight- or nine-figures.  And these cases are not rare.  More than 100 people die every week in truck crashes.  The broker’s insurance, by contrast, is often $10 to $25 million. These accidents are not inevitable.  Rather, they are often the consequence of persistent incentives favoring profits over safety and drivers.  Pay-by-the-mile compensation, for example, rewards long hours over sleep and safety.  Economic sociologist Steve Viscelli has documented how drivers turn to dangerous practices, including drug use, to stay awake, all to work more hours and earn more money.  Most companies turn a blind eye to such violations, welcoming the profits. The worst offenders are chameleon carriers: fleets that rack up safety violations, flout federal regulations, and, at the brink of collapse, reincarnate as new, “clean,” carriers, erasing their atrocious records.  Between 10% and 20% of the nation’s carriers operate somewhere on the chameleon carrier spectrum.  Daniel Sanchez, a driver of twenty-five years, described these carriers: “They don’t care if I got a violation or went to jail … the next day they’d have another driver in that truck. … You are not a human being for them.  You’re just a number.” Facing exploited drivers and judgment-proof carriers, the question becomes: who can be held liable for devastating crashes and interrelated dismal labor conditions?  Suits against sellers have largely failed as causation can be difficult to prove.  Sellers intentionally insulate themselves from liability through two middlemen (brokers and carriers).  In Miller v. C.H. Robinson, Inc., for example, a crash victim initially sued all four actors (seller, broker, driver, and carrier) but later dismissed claims against Costco, the seller.  Brokers may prove to strike the right balance: large enough to wield real influence and close enough to the harm to satisfy causation.  Yet several circuits have held that federal law preempts state-law challenges against brokers, leaving injured parties unable to sue them.  Last Term, the Supreme Court changed this. Broker Liability: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport In a unanimous 9-0 opinion, the Supreme Court held that state-law negligent-hiring claims against brokers are not preempted by federal law –– injured parties can in fact sue the broker. In Caribe Transport, a trucker veered off the road and struck Shawn Montgomery’s truck which was stopped on the shoulder.  Montgomery suffered severe injuries, including the amputation of his leg.  The driver worked for Caribe Transport, a carrier.  The country’s largest freight broker, C.H. Robinson, had coordinated the shipment.  Montgomery sued the driver, Caribe Transport, and C.H. Robinson, alleging that C.H. Robinson, negligently hired Caribe Transport despite its “conditional” safety rating; history of deficient drivers; and poor inspection, maintenance, and crash rate. C.H. Robinson argued that the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act (“FAAAA”) expressly preempted the claim.  The District Court and Seventh Circuit agreed.  Enacted in 1994, the FAAAA broadly preempts state laws related to trucker prices, routes, and services.  However, the statute contains an important exception: The preemption provision “shall not restrict the safety regulatory authority of a State with respect to motor vehicles” (emphasis added).  The question before the Court was whether Montgomery’s claim against the broker was “with respect to motor vehicles.”  The Court held that it was. The Court reasoned that Congress designed the FAAAA safety exception to ensure that preempting state economic regulation over motor vehicles did not restrict the “traditional state police power over safety” (i.e. traditional state sovereignty to promulgate safety regulations).  Taking a textualist approach, because the FAAAA does not define “with respect to,” the Court “g[a]ve the phrase its ordinary meaning” (“concerning” or “regarding”) and remarked that the Act defines “motor vehicle” broadly.  “Putting the pieces together,” a claim falls within the exception if it “‘concerns’ or ‘regards’ the vehicles used in transportation.”  Requiring a broker to exercise ordinary care in selecting a carrier, the Court concluded, “concerns” motor vehicles –– “most obviously, the trucks that will transport the goods.” Many labor groups have come out in support of the Court’s holding.  Teamsters General President Sean M. O’Brien praised the opinion: “[u]ntil now, … bad employers have been able to outsource their legal obligations to third parties because of a loophole in federal law.”  The Teamsters President continued, “[we] commend the Court for its decision, which will force the largest logistics employers in the country to finally prioritize worker and motorist safety over profits.” Brokers now have a strong incentive to do business with safe, reliable carriers.  Before, the fly-by-night carrier, with low capitalization, terrible working conditions, and a willingness to do anything for profits, had the advantage.  To brokers, it did not matter how the job got done, only that it got done.  Liability will mean that brokers can no longer turn a blind eye.  Instead, liability will increase the chances that safety, throughout the chain, becomes the priority.  As one driver put it, “[y]our safety record will be vital to your survival as a business.”  This protects not only other motorists but also workers, pushing out low-road employers who exploit their drivers, cut corners, and amass safety violations.  While Caribe Transport is a limited ruling –– the Court held only that claims against brokers may be brought, not that claims against brokers will win –– it remains a meaningful step to a trucking industry that is safe for all.
